title: What's inside a .dll
sub: Metadata: a program that describes itself
cards/0/body:
The output of compilation is called an assembly. It has two main layers:

CIL: what to do.
Metadata: what the program contains: which classes, and what methods and parameters they have.
cards/1/body: Like the packing list in a moving box. It lists both what's yours ("class Program, method Add") and what's borrowed, things the program takes from outside ("method WriteLine from the System.Console assembly").
cards/1/deep: These are the real metadata table names from the ECMA-335 standard. You can browse them in ildasm or ILSpy, or read them from code with System.Reflection.Metadata.
cards/2/q: Match each metadata table to what it holds
cards/2/pairs/1/1: This assembly's methods and their parameters
cards/2/pairs/2/1: Other code's methods that we call
cards/3/q: What does metadata describe? Select all that apply.
cards/3/explain: Metadata describes how the program is built. What happens at run time isn't in the file.
cards/4/body:
Since the packing list lives right in the file, you don't need separate description files. Older technologies like COM used IDL and type libraries for that.

Metadata powers IDE hints, the debugger and reflection, a program's way of looking at itself:
cards/5/q: How does the IDE know which methods a class in someone else's .dll has when there is no source?
cards/5/options/1: It guesses from the file name
cards/5/options/2: It downloads the source from the internet
cards/5/explain: The list of types and method signatures is in the metadata. The IDE simply reads it.
cards/6/q: Find the line that says "we call someone else's method"
cards/6/explain: MemberRef is a reference to a member of another type: here, Console.WriteLine from the System.Console assembly.
cards/7/body: An assembly is stored in the PE (Portable Executable) format, the same one regular Windows programs use. .NET extended it with a CLR header, metadata and CIL. That's how the system tells a .NET program from a regular one.
cards/8/q: Hello.dll was built on Windows and runs on Linux. Is it still a PE file?
cards/8/options/0: Yes, the assembly format is the same on every OS
cards/8/options/1: No, .NET repackages it into a Linux format
cards/8/options/2: No, on Linux assemblies are .so files
cards/8/explain: .NET assemblies are PE files on any OS. They are read by the CLR, not by the Linux loader.
cards/8/wrong/2: .so files are native Linux libraries. A .NET assembly stays a .dll with CIL inside.
